issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette:
Gerald Marsh is a 53-year-old married bus driver of Canadian descent who presented for psychological assessment following a sexual assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Gerald was raped by an acquaintance - a man he had known casually through a shared social group - during an evening when Gerald had stayed late after a gathering and fallen asleep on the man's couch, exhausted after a long shift. He woke to the assault already underway, disoriented, unable at first to understand what was happening. The sounds in the room - a particular kind of ambient noise, the creak of furniture, the man's breathing - are details that remain scorched into Gerald's memory with terrible clarity. He did not report the assault. He told no one, not even his wife, and returned to work within days, believing that silence was the only manageable path forward.

Gerald's symptoms emerged gradually but with gathering force over the weeks that followed. The memories do not arrive as ordinary recollections; he describes them as a film that plays on a loop, uninvited, vivid, and complete - and when they come, they bring with them the same terror he felt in those first disoriented moments of waking, as though no time has passed at all. Alongside that terror comes a wave of shame that he finds almost harder to bear - a visceral sense of disgust directed at his own body, a feeling that what happened to him has marked him in some permanent and humiliating way. He had come to believe, with quiet but absolute conviction, that his body had been made shameful, and this belief sat beneath his daily life like a fault line.

His occupation has become the central arena in which his symptoms play out most acutely. Every working day, Gerald drives a municipal bus - enclosed, populated, inescapable. The presence of passengers in his vehicle, people sitting behind him and around him, triggers intrusive recall with a reliability that has made each shift feel like an ordeal. The sounds of the bus itself - the hiss of the doors, the low mechanical hum - are close enough in register to the ambient sounds encoded in his traumatic memory that they pull him backward without warning, and the film begins again. His exhaustion compounds this: long shifts leave him depleted, and in that state of fatigue his defenses thin and the memories break through most forcefully, replicating something of the vulnerability he felt on the night of the assault. The tiredness itself has become a signal his nervous system reads as danger.

What has tightened the cycle most severely is the relationship between his appraisals and the memories they feed. Gerald had lost all faith in people - not as an abstract philosophical position, but as a lived, bodily certainty. He was convinced that people could not be trusted, that the assault had revealed something true about human nature that he had been naive to ignore. These beliefs, once established, coloured every face on his bus, every sound from behind him, until ordinary social proximity became saturated with threat. The mistrust sharpened his vigilance to the people around him while he drove, which meant that the very triggers embedded in his work environment were kept perpetually active. And as the mistrust and shame deepened, they seemed to make the memories more accessible, not less - as though the appraisals were continuously confirming the memories' relevance, keeping them from receding. The shame about his body, in particular, made it impossible to speak to his wife, and the silence between them had grown into something she had noticed and named, though she did not know its cause.

Gerald came to seek help after his supervisor placed him on a performance review following two incidents in which he had stopped the bus abruptly, unable to continue. He had managed, until then, to keep the extent of his distress invisible. What he fears most, sitting in the clinician's office, is that speaking about what happened will make the shame real in a new and permanent way. What he most hopes for, though he can barely articulate it, is to be able to drive again without the film starting - to be tired without it meaning something terrible is about to happen.
